readingInstruction: Read Esther 1:1-3:15. A Persian king deposes his queen, a Jewish orphan becomes queen, and a proud official plots to destroy the Jews. Notice what is missing from the book: God’s name is never mentioned.
settingTheScene: Esther is set in Susa, the Persian capital, around 483 to 473 BC, between the first return under Zerubbabel and the return under Ezra. Most Jews had stayed in the empire. The book is a story of those who remained scattered. It never names God, never mentions prayer except fasting, and yet shows his hand everywhere. The theme is “God unseen but sovereign.”
observation: “In those days, when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel” (1:2).
“For the queen’s behavior will become known to all women” (1:17).
“Mordecai… had taken her as his own daughter” (2:7).
“Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her” (2:10).
“And the king loved Esther more than all the women” (2:17).
“Mordecai told them that he was a Jew” (3:4).
“Haman… sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” (3:6).
“And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion” (3:15).
interpretation:
This is a story full of coincidences. The queen refuses to appear, so she is replaced, and a Jewish orphan girl is chosen. Her cousin Mordecai happens to overhear a plot against the king and reports it, and the deed is written in the chronicles. Haman is promoted. Mordecai refuses to bow, and Haman’s pride turns his anger against a whole people. He casts lots, called “pur,” to choose the day of destruction, and the lot falls on a date eleven months away.

The author never says “God did this.” Yet the reader sees a pattern: nothing is an accident. The Hebrew Bible keeps the name of God out of the text, but his purposes steer every scene. This is a book for people who live in a world where God seems silent. Most Jews of that age lived under pagan rule, far from the temple, with no prophet, no miracle, no visible sign. Esther says that God is still working.

There is a deeper background. Haman is an Agagite, a descendant of Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15). Mordecai is from the line of Kish, Saul’s father. The old conflict between Israel and Amalek, which Saul failed to finish, is reborn. The enemy of God’s people tries again to wipe them out. The question is whether God’s promise to Abraham, to bless the nations through his seed, will survive.

The edict goes out, and the chapter ends with an ugly picture: the king and Haman sit down to drink while the city is in confusion. The powerful feast while the powerless tremble.
connection: Romans 8:28 says that God works all things together for good. Genesis 50:20: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” Proverbs 16:33: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.” Exodus 17:14-16 is the LORD’s war against Amalek. Psalm 121:4: he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
application:
Where do you feel that God is silent in your life? Ask God to open your eyes to his unseen hand.

Look back at one “coincidence” in your story and thank God for it.

Pray for believers living under hostile or indifferent governments.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he rules even when his name is not spoken.
Ask him to open your eyes to his hand in your circumstances.
Tell him what feels like an accident in your life.
